title: Moment-Structured Block Encodings of Periodic Finite-Difference Operators
abstract: Block encoding is the standard technique for accessing matrix data in quantum linear-algebra algorithms. Its implementation directly affects its subnormalization, which in turn controls the algorithm's success probability, simulation time, and downstream costs. Explicit construction of block encodings with provably optimal subnormalization exists for only a handful of operators, with bespoke calculations used in its design. In this work, we develop a framework to block encode translation-invariant finite-difference operators on a periodic grid. These operators are the finite-difference discretizations of the constant-coefficient partial differential equations that sit at the core of scientific computing. We show that the moment order of these stencils can be used to simultaneously determine the continuum operator approximated, the vanishing order of the Fourier symbol, and the cost of the block encoding. From there, we derive a closed-form optimality criterion as a function of the stencil coefficients, which certifies whether the construction attains the optimal subnormalization for an entire operator family, uniformly in grid size, and quantifies the gap when it does not. The framework subsumes optimal constructions for the Laplacian operator in the literature and can be used to certify new instances at higher even orders, including the biharmonic operator. Furthermore, we derive success-probability floors parameterized by spectral properties of the operator's symbol and find explicit constants for the block encoding of the advection-diffusion family for which no prior explicit spatial block encoding exists.
summary: This work introduces a moment-structured framework to systematically block encode finite-difference approximations of PDEs for quantum computing. By linking the stencil's moment order ($m$) to its spectral properties and encoding cost, it provides an optimality criterion that certifies resource efficiency across entire families of operators. This advances the practical application of quantum algorithms to core scientific computations.
main_problem: Developing a unified framework to efficiently block encode translation-invariant finite-difference operators for use in quantum linear-algebra algorithms.
main_result: The moment order ($m$) of the stencil simultaneously determines the continuum operator approximated, the symbol's vanishing structure, and provides an explicit optimality criterion for the block encoding subnormalization.
method: The analysis uses moment theory to relate discrete stencils (spatial domain) to their Fourier symbols (spectral domain), allowing a unified characterization based on the moment order $m$.
model_or_system: The model involves discretizing constant-coefficient Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) on a periodic grid ($\mathbb{T}^d$) using finite-difference stencils, which are represented by shift-stencil operators.
key_observables: Subnormalization ($\lambda$), Moment Order ($m$), Success Probability ($	ext{psucc}$), and the Fourier symbol $b_H(k)$.
important_parameters: The moment order $m$ is central, governing the scaling of success probability ($\Theta(h^{2m})$) and the accuracy of the continuum approximation.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to translation-invariant operators with constant coefficients on a periodic grid; optimality criteria are derived under specific structural conditions.
figures_summary: Not specified by notes, but the structure implies showing how $m$ dictates the relationship between spatial stencils and spectral properties/encoding costs.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the problem (block encoding of PDEs) to establishing moment theory links (spatial $\leftrightarrow$ spectral), deriving the optimality criterion based on $m$, and finally applying this framework to specific families like Laplacian and advection-diffusion operators.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, systematic method to analyze the quantum resource cost associated with simulating fundamental PDEs using quantum algorithms, directly impacting algorithm feasibility.
